claims.text: The disordered high-entropy alloy has significant local magnetic fluctuations arising from its mixture of transition metals.
Local magnetic fluctuations inhibit conventional superconducting pairing.
Thermal annealing will promote subtle or short-range atomic ordering without changing the alloy's overall composition.
Annealing-induced atomic ordering will reduce the density of magnetic scattering or fluctuation centers.
Reducing magnetic scattering centers will enhance electron-phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling and reduced magnetic scattering will permit Cooper pairing at low temperature.
The starting material is an as-cast, single-phase high-entropy alloy with a random elemental distribution.
Co, Cr, and Mn in the starting alloy act as magnetic constituents contributing to local magnetic fluctuations.
The annealing treatment can be tuned to induce ordering without causing large-scale phase separation or precipitate formation.
Peak sharpening in X-ray diffraction can be used as an indicator of increased local atomic ordering in this alloy.
Transmission electron microscopy and magnetic susceptibility can assess local ordering and suppression of magnetic clusters.
Disordered magnetic moments in the as-cast alloy cause scattering that breaks Cooper pairs.
Annealed samples will have a higher critical temperature than as-cast samples.
Annealed samples will exhibit a sharper and more pronounced resistive superconducting transition than as-cast samples.
The as-cast alloy will show either no superconductivity or a very low critical temperature with a broad transition.
Strong magnetic fluctuations are responsible for the absent, low-temperature, or broad superconducting transition expected in the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains single-phase and lacks significant compositional segregation.
Electron-phonon coupling is likely the dominant pairing mechanism below approximately 10 K in the selected alloy.
As-cast and annealed samples from the same batch will be compared using identical low-temperature resistivity and magnetic-susceptibility measurements.
The hypothesis is falsified if annealing produces neither a significant improvement in the superconducting transition nor a reduction in measured magnetic fluctuations.
